title: 13 Effect of supplementation frequency of cottonseed meal to pre-pubertal heifers consuming low quality forage
content:
Abstract
In semi-arid regions, grasses mature quickly and quality declines with it, leaving low quality standing hay which is not typically suitable for growing calves. Research has demonstrated that cattle grazing low quality forage can benefit from protein supplementation since overall crude protein is typically limiting optimal ruminal fermentation of fiber. However, frequent supplementation increases labor costs. Although ruminants can recycle nitrogen in protein limiting environments it is not clear how frequently pre-pubertal replacement heifers must be supplemented to maintain acceptable feeding and growth performance. Our objective was to determine the optimal supplementation frequency of cottonseed meal to heifers consuming a low quality forage. Sixty prepubertal Angus heifers between the ages of 7 and 9 months weighing 278 ± 4 kg were blocked by body weight (light and heavy) and sorted into 6 pens equipped with C-Lock SmartFeeders for automated intake monitoring for 56 days. Pens within blocks were randomly assigned to treatment groups so that each treatment received a diet of low quality forage (6.3% CP) and approximately 18% CSM (48% CP) to allow an overall diet of 12.66% CP where: CSM1 (daily supplementation of protein), CSM2 (supplemented every two days with equivalent daily protein delivery), and CSM4 (supplemented every 4 days with equivalent daily protein delivery). Heifers were evaluated for growth of ribeye area, rib fat, and rump fat, using ultrasound on days 0, and 56 of the trial. Feeding and growth performance variables were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS v.9 where treatment and weight block were fixed effects and pen was a random effect. Per design there was no treatment difference in initial body weight of heifers, however, there was a tendency for heifers in the CSM2 treatment group to have a slightly larger ribeye area (P = 0.08) and slightly greater rump fat (P = 0.07) than CSM1 and CSM4 which was not accounted for when blocking for body weight differences. There was no treatment effect on mid-test body weight but final body weight was greater for CSM1 and CSM2 than CSM4 (306 and 303.2 vs. 289.6 kg, respectively; P=0.033). This was likely a response of the treatment effect on ADG where CSM1 and CSM2 performed greater than CSM4 (P= 0.0001). Heifers in CSM2 had greater DMI than CSM1 and CSM4 (7.63 vs. 6.75 and 6.57 kg, respectively; P = 0.0031). Feed efficiency was greatest for CSM1 and CSM2 versus CSM4 (0.028 and 0.029 vs. 0.017 kg, respectively; P = 0.0016). There was no difference in final ribeye area, rib fat, or rump fat between treatments. Although the equivalent protein was delivered to all heifers, it appears that a 4 day frequency may reduce feeding and growth performance but may not alter body composition.
